gummed up, that is, with a gunky substance called amyloid,

Rebecca Gottesman was one of the researchers.

Thank you. Thanks for having me.
I thought this was a done deal,
that we knew that if you had coronary risk factors in midlife,
it stuffed up your brain in late life.

Well, we did know from studies, including my own,
as well as other studies done by other terrific groups, that vascular risk factors, heart risk
factors, as you mentioned, are associated with bad outcomes in terms of both your cognition as well

know that heart risks increase risk of dementia, what we haven't understood is, is it just that you
happen to have two things going on in your brain? You have Alzheimer's type changes and you have
vascular type changes, that your cognition might be worse and you might be more likely to be
given a diagnosis of dementia? Or is it that the vascular changes are actually doing something in
the brain that triggers Alzheimer's neuropathology? And our study where we use PET imaging, looking at
amyloid deposition in the brain specifically, suggests that there may be a direct effect of
these vascular risk factors on the Alzheimer's pathology. So PET is like a nuclear scan which
shows the brain in action, that shows the metabolism of the sugar in the brain actively.
So it's unlike an MRI, which is more static, a PET is more dynamic.
Exactly.
And specifically with PET, you can look not only at sugar in the brain, as you mentioned,
but other types of markers.
So in this particular study, we looked at a specific marker called forbetapir, which
we think binds to amyloid in the brain.
And the leading hypothesis of Alzheimer's is that amyloid builds up to lead to Alzheimer's.
So in this particular study, we can inject this isotope through an IV when people are
getting a PET scan, and it binds to the parts of the brain where there's amyloids specifically.
And these were people who didn't have dementia in this particular study, but we found that a
number of them still had higher levels of amyloid than would be considered normal.
So tell us a bit more about the study. Who did you study and what did you do?
Sure. So the atherosclerosis risk and community study, or the ARIC study,
has been going on now for nearly 30 years. It was initiated in four community sites across
the United States. This study started evaluating nearly 16,000 people almost 30 years ago and has
followed them over time, collected important information about vascular risk factors,
vascular markers, followed them for cognitive function at a few earlier time points. And most
recently in 2011 to 2013, people had a more detailed cognitive assessment in a subset of
people had brain MRIs. And then I recruited from that subset to do these PET scans. So these are
people who don't have dementia but were recruited from the community 30 years ago. We have all of
this longitudinal information about them, and now we have this PET amyloid imaging on this subset of
346 people in whom we can really look at the relationship. And what risk factors did you look
at? So we focused on five risk factors, and a key point I want to make is that we looked at their
status in middle age, so at the first visit in the ARIC study, which is when people were 45 to 64
four years old, because some evidence has suggested that midlife risk factors are even
more important for later life dementia as opposed to risk factors later. So we looked at high blood
pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, and smoking status when people were middle-aged,
and we found that the more risk factors you had, the more amyloid you had in your brain.
Specifically, when we looked at the individual risk factors, the only one that was associated
with amyloid later was obesity. The other ones didn't have a separate effect, but really the
cumulative amount of these risk factors appear to be most important. So let me just get that
straight about obesity. So obesity was the one that counted later in life rather than in midlife.
Is that what you were saying? No. So obesity was the one that when we looked at them individually
in midlife, it had an effect by itself. Ah, I see. The rest were working together. Exactly. So
hypertension, there was a suggestion of an increased risk, but statistically it didn't
show an association with amyloid. Obesity did, but just from midlife. Which ties in with essentially
evidence-based practice now where people say, look, your cholesterol doesn't matter that much
by itself or your blood pressure doesn't matter that much by itself, but it's your total risk
when you add up all the factors. That's what counts, your so-called absolute risk. So in other words,
what you're saying here is that your absolute risk, your total risk of heart disease also
affects your brain. Absolutely. And the problem is a lot of these risk factors do go together,
though. So it's not that common that someone just has one of them. So it's pretty common that these
co-occur, which means that it's going to be common that people have an elevated risk associated with
that co-occurrence. Now, there have been studies of amyloid in the brain, which suggests you can
find people with a lot of amyloid in the brain and no dementia and no cognitive problems.
And there's still a lot of debate about whether amyloid really matters much at all.
Is this a stepping stone on the way to cognitive decline, or is it just something else you've found?
I think that's a great point, and you're absolutely right. Our study is an example of the fact that
people can have elevated amyloid and be non-demented. So there's people in our study who
had mild cognitive impairment, but no one who had dementia. We also had people who were totally
normal, and some of those had elevated amyloid. So amyloid is but one factor in the pathway of
things that leads to Alzheimer's, and it may just be a marker of the other things that have happened.
Regardless, I think these data suggest the importance of looking decades earlier than
the amyloid changes. So we know that in Alzheimer's disease, part of the reason that treatment
attempts have been unsuccessful to date and that there's no known way to prevent or treat Alzheimer's
is because we're probably looking at people a little bit too late. So we're looking at them
when they already have amyloid in the brain or there's already tau. Which is the other piece of
exactly the other big factor. So there's been an emphasis in Alzheimer's community at looking at
people before clinical disease and our data suggests that if vascular risk factors are
playing an important role, you really need to look decades before you start having even amyloid
changes. But you're absolutely right, figuring out how tau fits in and other changes in the brain,
inflammatory changes, etc. There's likely many things going on. I still think this is probably
a piece of the puzzle, not a solution to the puzzle. But I do think it's an important part
in understanding what's happening in Alzheimer's. So does it shine a light on the cause of
Alzheimer's? I think that it shines a light on vascular risk factors as maybe having a direct
impact on Alzheimer's. And I'm not going to say this tells us that the cause of Alzheimer's is
vascular disease, because it certainly doesn't. But I do think it gives important information that
it may directly affect the pathology that leads to Alzheimer's, as opposed to just being another
bystander that if you happen to have both, your cognition will be worse. Now, there is a gene
that increases your risk of Alzheimer's disease, and it's related to vascular risk factors, and
it's called APOE4. Did you do any sub-studies on this group of people for their APOE4 status to
see whether that further boosted their deposition of amyloid? We did. So our studies have certainly
verified the fact in this cohort that having an E4 allele, that particular type of the APOE gene,
does increase risk, as we would expect, also increases the amount of amyloid. So in other
studies, increased risk of dementia, and in this particular Eric Pett study that I've been
describing, it increased risk of amyloid. We looked specifically at that exact question to see how
having an APOE E4 gene changed the way vascular risk affected amyloid. And we didn't find a
statistical difference in people who were carriers of an E4 gene and those who weren't.
Both groups had an elevated risk associated with more vascular risk factors. There's sort of a hint
that maybe people who were gene carriers had an even higher risk, but statistically, we didn't
have enough power to show that difference. So we can't say with confidence that the combination
vascular risk factors and having ApoE, E4 allele, and this increased genetic risk increases your
risk that much more. But the data do suggest that there might be something there with that
particular combination. So if you're in your 70s, is there any point to changing your risk factors
then if you're looking to protect your brain, given that there's very little evidence that it
has an impact? I still think that there is. And obviously, the jury is still a little bit out on
at what age it becomes maybe dangerous to treat some of these. So hypertension be an example.
in the U.S. there was a sort of set of guidelines for hypertension treatment that initially said

look at cognition specifically in association with that tighter blood pressure control but I think
There's other ways in which vascular risk factors can adversely affect the brain.

Absolutely. And so that's further evidence supporting this general idea that risk factors
